title: Textual Variants Explained
subtitle: How differences between copies affect confidence in particular passages
summary: A textual variant is a difference between witnesses, not a verdict that a whole scripture is unknowable. The endings of Mark and the woman accused of adultery show why some biblical passages require critical judgment. Quranic readings and manuscripts also contain variation; a fair comparison asks about its kind, date, scale, and transmission rather than pretending one side has none.

seo.metaTitle: Textual Variants Explained: Bible Manuscripts vs. The Quran's Text
seo.metaDescription: How manuscript differences affect particular passages, with Mark and John as examples and the same standards applied to Quranic evidence.

sections.title: A Difference Is the Beginning of the Question
sections.body:
If two copies differ, at least one cannot reproduce the same wording at that point. That matters. It does not follow that every sentence in either copy is uncertain or that the entire religion was invented.

Textual criticism compares witnesses to identify early wording and explain later differences. Its results can be strong, probable, or unresolved. The honest task is to match confidence to the actual passage.

sections.title: Why Copies Differ
sections.body:
A copyist may skip between similar phrases, repeat a line, modernize spelling, harmonize parallel accounts, or incorporate a marginal explanation. Some changes are accidental; others are deliberate. Motive should not be asserted without evidence.

Counting every difference gives little guidance by itself. Many late copies can multiply the same change, and many spelling differences can leave the meaning intact. A short addition affecting a major claim can matter more than hundreds of harmless spelling differences.

sections.title: Apply the Standard to the Quran Too
sections.body:
Quran 15:9 states the promise of protection. Muslim belief accepts canonical readings as authorized parts of transmission. That theological judgment should not be confused with the descriptive fact that readings can differ.

The Quranic record includes spelling differences, copyists' mistakes, canonical word and grammatical variants, and some early nonstandard textual evidence. [Qira'at Explained Simply](/articles/qiraat-explained-simply) distinguishes those categories. A comparison built on 'Bible variants versus no Quran variants' would begin with a false premise.

sections.title: Two Larger Examples Readers Can Check
sections.body:
Mark 16:9–20 is the longer ending printed in many Bibles. The [Catholic note](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/mark/16) distinguishes it from Mark's ending at 16:8 while acknowledging its early reception and canonical status in that church.

John 7:53–8:11, the woman accused of adultery, also has a complex transmission history. The [Catholic note on John 8](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/john/8) identifies it as a later insertion and still recognizes it as canonical scripture. Here the questions 'was it in the earliest recoverable form?' and 'does this church accept it?' are visibly different.

sections.title: How Editors Reach a Judgment
sections.body:
Scholars weigh a witness's age, its relationship to others, geographical spread where known, and which reading best explains the alternatives. The oldest surviving copy is important but not automatically correct at every point.

The Quran's dominant manuscripts reflect an early standard; biblical textual study often compares a broader range of copied forms. That is a meaningful historical difference. It is not permission to compare an ideal account of Quranic transmission with only the worst biblical examples.

sections.title: The Strongest Christian Reply
sections.body:
A Christian may say that disputed passages are openly marked and that the resurrection, for example, is not based solely on Mark's longer ending. That is correct. Recognizing this variant does not erase the other Gospel narratives or Paul's testimony.

The remaining issue is narrower but real: a verse should not be defended as unquestionably original wording merely because a familiar Bible prints it. An argument about a doctrine must be reassessed if it depends specifically on disputed wording. Other evidence for the doctrine must then be considered on its merits.

sections.title: Why Early Stabilization Still Matters
sections.body:
An early shared written framework reduces the range that must be reconstructed later. That is a genuine strength in the Quran's preservation case, especially alongside learned recitation. It does not prove the text divine or answer every question about its early readings.

Islam can make an affirmative case for reliable access without claiming every biblical teaching is lost. [How Was the Quran Preserved?](/articles/how-was-the-quran-preserved) explains that case with its qualifications.

sections.title: Use Footnotes as Evidence, Not Ammunition
sections.body:
When a footnote names a variant, read it and the surrounding passage. Ask what changes, how the evidence is weighed, and whether your belief depends on that wording. A disclosed uncertainty is useful information.

For the different question of which books a church accepts, continue with [Biblical Canon Formation](/articles/biblical-canon-formation). A variant within a book is not the same issue as the boundary of a canon.

sections.title: The Four Details a Good Claim Supplies
sections.body: Identify the passage, the competing forms, the witnesses supporting each, and the effect on meaning. A claim missing these details may be too vague to evaluate. This applies equally to a sensational allegation against the Quran and a reassurance that no biblical text ever changed.

sections.title: Begin With the Textual Notes
sections.body: The linked editions above let you inspect two concrete cases. The textbook below explains the method; Bruce gives a Christian defense of the documentary evidence. Reading both is more informative than using a raw variant count as a verdict.

She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. When they heard that he was alive, and had been seen by her, they disbelieved. After these things he was revealed in another form to two of them, as they walked, on their way into the country. They went away and told it to the rest. They didn’t believe them, either. Afterward he was revealed to the eleven themselves as they sat at the table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they didn’t believe those who had seen him after he had risen. He said to them, “Go into all the world, and preach the Good News to the whole creation. He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who disbelieves will be condemned. These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak with new languages; they will take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it will in no way hurt them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will recover.” So then the Lord, after he had spoken to them, was received up into heaven, and sat down at the right hand of God. They went out, and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them, and confirming the word by the signs that followed. Amen.
Everyone went to his own house,

but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. Now very early in the morning, he came again into the temple, and all the people came to him. He sat down, and taught them. The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman taken in adultery. Having set her in the middle, they told him, “Teacher, we found this woman in adultery, in the very act. Now in our law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. What then do you say about her?” They said this testing him, that they might have something to accuse him of. But Jesus stooped down, and wrote on the ground with his finger. But when they continued asking him, he looked up and said to them, “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her.” Again he stooped down, and with his finger wrote on the ground. They, when they heard it, being convicted by their conscience, went out one by one, beginning from the oldest, even to the last. Jesus was left alone with the woman where she was, in the middle. Jesus, standing up, saw her and said, “Woman, where are your accusers? Did no one condemn you?” She said, “No one, Lord.” Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. faq.question: Do variants make the entire Bible unknowable?
faq.answer: No. Many passages are well supported; some have uncertain details, and a smaller group involves larger additions or omissions. The conclusion must be specific.

faq.question: Are Mark's longer ending and the woman accused of adultery hidden?
faq.answer: No. Many modern editions print them with brackets or notes, and critical scholarship discusses them openly. Printing and canonical acceptance are different from a claim of original authorship.

faq.question: Does removing Mark's longer ending remove the resurrection from Christianity?
faq.answer: No. Other Gospel passages and earlier Christian testimony remain. This variant concerns particular wording and attribution, not the disappearance of the whole Christian argument.

faq.question: Does the Quran also have variants?
faq.answer: Yes. The categories include spelling, copying errors, received reading differences, and some early nonstandard evidence. Their authorization and historical relationships require explanation, not denial.

faq.question: Is the oldest manuscript always right?
faq.answer: No. Age is important, but an early copy can contain an error and a later copy can preserve an earlier reading. Relationships among witnesses also matter.
